content: Women who were breastfeeding were excluded from the study due to uncertainties regarding the safety of the drugs rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide in this population. If a woman became pregnant while receiving the study regimen, she was withdrawn from the study and treated according to national tuberculosis (TB) program guidelines or local protocols. These women continued to attend scheduled study follow-ups but were classified as being on a non-study regimen and did not undergo study-related radiographic evaluations. Similarly, women who became pregnant during the follow-up period (but not while on study treatment) continued with scheduled follow-ups but were not subjected to study radiographs. Regardless of whether pregnancy occurred during treatment or follow-up, the outcomes of the pregnancies were documented in the study records. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) discussed several implementation considerations. One key topic was drug susceptibility testing (DST). The panel emphasized the importance of striving for universal DST within national TB programs. While universal DST may not always be feasible, rapid DST for critical drugs such as rifampicin, isoniazid, and fluoroquinolones is increasingly available and expanding rapidly. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends rapid genotypic testing for TB and rifampicin resistance as an initial diagnostic test. If the same sputum sample can also be tested for susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and isoniazid, this would enable the selection of the most effective treatment regimen. However, this approach has logistical, laboratory workload, and cost implications. The panel acknowledged that while universal DST is desirable, baseline DST for fluoroquinolones may not be essential when patients undergo WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic tests for rifampicin resistance. In settings with high fluoroquinolone resistance among new TB patients, baseline DST for fluoroquinolones is strongly recommended. Directly observed treatment (DOT) was another consideration. In the trial, patients received daily treatment under direct observation at least five days per week. However, this level of supervision may not be feasible in routine programmatic settings. DOT is particularly important given the high pill burden and the absence of a fixed-dose combination formulation for the regimen. It also serves as a measure to prevent the amplification of drug resistance. Current WHO recommendations support the use of DOT alongside other forms of patient support. Despite the shorter duration of the four-month regimen compared to the standard six-month regimen, patient support remains a critical component of TB care. The pill burden for the four-month regimen is currently higher than that of the standard regimen due to the lack of a fixed-dose combination tablet and the high dose of rifapentine (1200 mg). This may affect patient acceptability, although this situation could improve in the future as the regimen gains wider adoption, creating demand for its components. The availability of a 300 mg rifapentine formulation could reduce the pill burden and facilitate implementation until a fixed-dose combination tablet becomes available. The cost of the shorter regimen is significantly higher than the standard regimen, primarily due to the inclusion of rifapentine. However, as the regimen becomes more widely adopted, the cost may decrease due to increased demand for the drugs. Administering the shorter regimen with food may pose challenges in some settings. In the trial, a flat dose of 1200 mg of rifapentine was administered daily with food. This dosing strategy was based on evidence from phase I and II trials demonstrating the safety of rifapentine at this dose, the minimal impact of body weight on rifapentine clearance, the enhancement of rifapentine absorption with food, and pharmacokinetic modeling predictions that the target rifapentine exposure (area under the curve [AUC] of approximately 500–600 mcgh/L) could be achieved with this approach. The strategy of dosing with food was chosen because requiring a very high-fat meal was deemed impractical in both trial and routine TB care settings. Training healthcare workers was identified as another critical implementation consideration. Introducing the shorter regimen into programmatic settings will require training, but this is a standard requirement for any new intervention. The potential to shorten treatment and treat more patients may offset the initial investment in training. The GDG also discussed the choice of regimen for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB). When deciding between the shorter four-month regimen and the standard six-month regimen, clinicians should consider eligibility criteria, patient preferences, and local factors such as the availability of rifapentine. For children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB (without suspicion or evidence of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB), a four-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) is recommended. Non-severe TB is defined as peripheral lymph node TB, intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease confined to one lung lobe without a miliary pattern. Children who do not meet the criteria for non-severe TB should receive the standard six-month regimen (2HRZE/4HR) or regimens recommended for severe forms of extrapulmonary TB. The use of ethambutol during the first two months of treatment is recommended in settings with a high prevalence of HIV or isoniazid resistance. The SHINE trial (Shorter Treatment for Minimal Tuberculosis in Children) was the first large phase III trial to evaluate the duration of TB treatment in children with non-severe drug-susceptible TB. The trial compared a four-month regimen to the standard six-month regimen in children under 16 years of age. The trial demonstrated that the shorter regimen was non-inferior to the standard regimen in terms of treatment outcomes. The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of treatment failure, loss to follow-up, TB recurrence, or death by 72 weeks. The primary safety outcome was the occurrence of grade 3–5 adverse events during treatment. The trial included 1204 children, with a median age of 5 years, 52% of whom were male, 11% living with HIV, and 14% with bacteriologically confirmed TB. Retention and adherence rates were high, at 95% and 94%, respectively. The shorter regimen was associated with similar rates of adverse events compared to the standard regimen. The GDG concluded that the shorter regimen offers several advantages, including reduced treatment duration, lower costs for families and health systems, and potentially improved adherence. However, the balance of effects did not strongly favor either the shorter or longer regimen, as both were effective. The GDG emphasized the importance of considering cost, acceptability, and feasibility when implementing the shorter regimen.
